item.description:

Upskilling health professionals to deliver emotional well-being support for people with diabetes

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

For more than 1.5 million Australians living with diabetes, managing their condition is a relentless, 24-hour responsibility. Day after day, people are required to make decisions about medications, glucose monitoring, food, physical activity and other aspects of their care—largely outside the health care system.

This substantial and often unseen work is fundamental to living well with diabetes and reducing the risk of complications. Yet the emotional burden it places on people is too often overlooked.

As health psychology researcher Dr. Edith Holloway, Deakin Institute for Health Transformation (DIHT) senior research fellow at The Australian Center for Behavioral Research in Diabetes (ACBRD), explains, "Up to one in two people with diabetes experience mental health and emotional challenges, such as diabetes distress, which affects their ability to self-manage their condition.

"When people are struggling emotionally, it can become much harder to manage medications, glucose levels, eating, physical activity and engagement with health professionals—this impacts their diabetes health outcomes and can increase the risk of complications."

Inadequate emotional support undermines diabetes self-management

Currently, diabetes costs the Australian health system AU$14.2 billion. Projections indicate the number of Australians living with diabetes will double to 3 million by 2030, increasing the pressure on diabetes services and the broader Australian health system.

Without emotional support to ease diabetes distress and encourage self-management, people with diabetes face increased risk of emergency admissions, hospitalizations and long-term complications. This includes people with limited access to face-to-face diabetes care, such as people living in remote and rural Australia.

"From our needs assessments, we know people with diabetes want to talk to their diabetes health professionals about the emotional side of living with diabetes. We know emotional challenges can be supported during routine diabetes care before they escalate to mental health conditions, which are more costly to the health system and require specialist care."

Upskilling more diabetes health professionals to deliver LISTEN

Because diabetes educators, nurses and dietitians understand the complexities of living with diabetes, they are well positioned as trusted health care professionals to provide timely emotional support to people with diabetes before problems escalate.

The proven early intervention LISTEN (Low-Intensity Support To ENhance emotional well-being in diabetes care) reduces diabetes distress, increases emotional well-being and improves diabetes self-management.

To develop a larger workforce to provide emotional support to more people with diabetes, health professionals can now upskill in LISTEN via a two-stage structured training and accreditation pathway.

The first stage is a self-paced LISTEN e-learning course that provides a foundation for understanding diabetes distress and low-intensity emotional support. This course helps participants develop practical interpersonal skills, including empathy, reflective listening, validating emotions and person-centered communication that can be applied immediately to routine care.

Holloway and fellow researchers at the ACBRD, Deakin University and DIHT co-developed the self-paced course in partnership with Diabetes Victoria. Moving this foundational component from in-person workshops to e-learning makes the training more accessible and gives busy health professionals greater flexibility to complete it around their clinical commitments.

Health professionals seeking to become accredited LISTEN facilitators undertake a second stage of further training, including supervised practice, where they demonstrate they can competently deliver the intervention in accordance with the LISTEN framework.

Aspiring to support all Australians living with diabetes

Importantly, the Australian Diabetes Educators Association (ADEA), the nation's peak body for diabetes education, management and care, has endorsed the online course.

Holloway said scaling and translating the program into routine care is a key piece of the commercialization strategy: "We can't provide LISTEN to all Australians with diabetes if we don't have the health workforce trained and upskilled in how to deliver it."

Workforce upskilling reaches more people with diabetes

While the LISTEN e-learning course is still in its early post-launch marketing phase, ADEA's endorsement and promotion to its more than 3,000 health professional members, including around 2,000 diabetes educators, strengthens LISTEN's impact.

"People with diabetes have been asking for emotional support for a long time. And health professionals want to support their patients and clients, but currently don't have the skills, resources and tools to do that. LISTEN addresses this gap in diabetes care. We have the capability now, with this training, to support around 750,000 Australians who are experiencing emotional challenges," said Holloway.

Better coping for healthier outcomes

In a recent trial, people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes who accessed up to four LISTEN sessions via a trained LISTEN facilitator had significant reductions in diabetes distress, as well as significant improvements in emotional well-being and coping skills, compared to a matched group receiving routine diabetes care.

"The LISTEN program helped people with diabetes be more engaged with their health professionals—exercising more, eating healthier food, monitoring glucose levels more regularly and taking their medication when required. The impact of enhancing all these self-management behaviors is critical for improving physical and clinical outcomes, as well as potential cost savings."

Holloway recently shared her team's research on mental health in diabetes care with government policymakers to help them understand the program's health sector and societal cost benefits. Economic modeling showed that scaling LISTEN nationally could generate AU$2.1 billion in net savings by preventing crisis care, cutting avoidable health system costs and boosting productivity.

Ideally, making LISTEN sessions available for Australians through diabetes services and the Medicare-supported Chronic Condition Management Plan would expand emotional support for people with diabetes and broaden the program's impact. "It's a big undertaking to lobby the government. We've had conversations around the policy implications, and it's something we're working toward."

item.description:

Major data gap for gut disorders leaves Aotearoa in the dark

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

A lack of up-to-date New Zealand research into common gut disorders means the country is effectively flying blind on conditions that may affect about 1 in 3 adults, University of Otago research suggests.

Dr. Simone Bayer and research colleagues from the University of Otago have reviewed all available evidence in Aotearoa on disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI)—a group of chronic conditions including irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional dyspepsia. Their findings, published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, reveal a striking lack of contemporary data on how common these conditions are, who is affected and what costs they incur to our health system.

Only four New Zealand studies reporting the prevalence of DGBI were identified, with the most recent published in 2002. The studies were limited to Wellington and Dunedin, and none provided prevalence data for Māori or Pacific peoples.

"People living with these conditions can experience significant and ongoing symptoms, yet we don't have any strong contemporary evidence telling us how many New Zealanders are affected," Bayer says. "That means we are also unable to properly comprehend the scale of demand on our health system, or whether different groups of New Zealanders are experiencing these conditions and accessing care in different ways."

DGBI, formerly known as functional gastrointestinal disorders, affect the way the gut functions without an identifiable structural or organic disease being found. Symptoms can include abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits and indigestion.

Internationally, the conditions are common. Research from the United Kingdom and Australia (which both have comparable publicly funded health systems) using contemporary diagnostic criteria found that approximately 37% of adults meet the criteria for at least one DGBI.

Using U.K. estimates of direct health care costs for IBS as a conservative proxy, the researchers estimate that if one-third of New Zealand's adult population has a DGBI, direct health care costs could be about NZ$1.6 billion a year.

Bayer stresses that this is a modeled estimate, rather than a direct measurement of New Zealand's current costs. "However, even this conservative estimate points to a substantial burden. The important message is that we simply do not have the New Zealand data needed to understand the problem properly," she explains.

The researchers found the evidence gap is particularly concerning for Māori, with no study identified measuring DGBI prevalence in Māori. They say future research should be designed from the outset to produce Māori-specific estimates and be undertaken in partnership with Māori health researchers and communities.

The paper also highlights the potential economic consequences of DGBI, which can involve repeated primary care visits, specialist referrals, investigations and medication, as well as lost productivity through absenteeism, reduced productivity at work and leaving the workforce early.

Bayer says the findings demonstrate the need for dedicated research investment. "We need to know how common these conditions really are in Aotearoa, how they affect different communities and what they are costing patients and the health system," she says. "A national prevalence study, alongside a formal analysis of health care costs using New Zealand health data, would give us the evidence needed to improve diagnosis, treatment and planning."

Publication details

Simone Bayer et al., Disorders of gut–brain interaction in Aotearoa New Zealand: a long-standing evidence gap with unmeasured health and economic consequences, New Zealand Medical Journal (2026). DOI: 10.26635/6965.7608

Journal information: New Zealand Medical Journal

'Pan-RAS molecular glue' is a safe and effective treatment for lung and pancreatic cancers

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Results from the AURORAS-1 Phase I clinical trial of an anticancer drug called ERAS-0015 have shown that it is safe and has caused tumors to shrink in hard-to-treat diseases such as lung and pancreatic cancer.

Presented at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain, the findings from 148 patients are significant because ERAS-0015 targets tumors whose growth is driven by mutations in the RAS gene. Until recently, it was not thought possible to design drugs that could target these mutations successfully.

Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute, Sarasota, U.S., told the symposium, "AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients who have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer.

"A 'response' means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer.

"In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects."

ERAS-0015 is a "pan-RAS molecular glue," which means that it brings proteins together at the molecular level in a way that blocks tumor growth signals from several different cancer-driving RAS mutations. Certain RAS mutations work like a switch that is locked in the "on" position, continuously conveying signals that lead to and sustain cancer. ERAS-0015 is designed to bind to the RAS "switch" while it is in the 'on' state and thereby blocks those signals.

"The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient's mutation, or the 'Achilles heel' of a specific individual's cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations," said Wang.

The AURORAS-1 trial started in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 on its own and in combination with other anticancer therapies in people living with several types of RAS-mutant solid tumors. Enrolled patients have non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has started to spread beyond the site of the primary tumor (locally advanced or metastatic), pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer and other solid tumors.

The results presented were for 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC; the trial is continuing to enroll patients.

Doses of ERAS-0015 started at 2 mg and increased up to 40 mg. During an average (median) follow-up period of just over four months, there was no sign that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients (44%) with pancreatic cancer who received 32 mg of ERAS-0015 and who had been previously treated with chemotherapy. Tumors shrank in three of five patients (60%) with lung cancer who received 32 mg and who had been treated previously with an immune checkpoint inhibitor or platinum-based chemotherapy.

The most common adverse side effects at doses of 16–32 mg in 10% or more of patients were rash, diarrhea, nausea and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) reported severe (grade 3 or higher) treatment-related side effects. No side effects limited the drug doses.

"We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients who have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer," said Wang.

"Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options."

Limitations of the study are those associated with Phase I trials that always include only a limited number of patients. Further study in greater numbers of patients and in Phase II and III clinical trials is needed to confirm the safety and efficacy of ERAS-0015.

"If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1," she concluded.

Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d'Hebron Institute of Oncology's clinical research program, was not involved with the study.

She commented, "This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging antitumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

"This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently."

More information

Preliminary safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of ERAS-0015: Results from the AURORAS-1 first-in-human trial, 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics, Barcelona, Spain, 18–20 November 2026.

Source: Medical Xpress | Published: 2026-11-21 02:40 UTC

Mental health diagnoses rise with medical complexity, chronicity in children

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

The prevalence of mental health (MH) diagnoses increases with increasing medical complexity and chronicity in Medicaid-enrolled children, according to a study published in Pediatrics.

Maria Newmaster, M.D., from Children's Mercy Kansas City in Missouri, and colleagues compared the prevalence of MH diagnoses across categories of complex and chronic conditions in a retrospective cross-sectional study of 2.9 million children aged 5 to 17 years from the Marketscan Medicaid Database in 2022.

The presence of a mood or anxiety MH diagnosis (anxiety, depression, bipolar, obsessive-compulsive disorders, trauma-related disorders and suicide/self-injury) coded at one inpatient/emergency department or two outpatient encounters was examined as the outcome.

The researchers observed an increase in the prevalence of MH diagnoses with increasing medical complexity and chronicity: 7.6%, 16.0% and 20.0% in noncomplex/nonchronic conditions, noncomplex chronic conditions (NCCCs) and complex chronic conditions (CCCs), respectively.

Among children with a CCC, the cardiac, neurologic and renal categories had the greatest odds of MH diagnoses (odds ratios, 1.49, 1.18 and 1.13, respectively). Compared with non-Hispanic white children, Black and Hispanic children had lower odds of MH diagnoses among youth with NCCCs or CCCs.

"These results carry profound implications given the associated increased risk of health care utilization, economic burden, disease exacerbation and poor quality of life," the authors write.

"Understanding specific NCCC and CCC categories and sociodemographic characteristics of patients at greatest odds of having comorbid MH conditions may enable clinicians to improve screening and intervention efforts and promote health equity among medically vulnerable populations."

Publication details

Maria Newmaster et al., Mental Health Diagnoses Among Children With and Without Complex and Chronic Conditions, Pediatrics (2026). DOI: 10.1542/peds.2026-076830

Journal information: Pediatrics

NI doctors' strike due to end, with separate walkout planned for Monday

- Published

A 24-hour strike by resident doctors in Northern Ireland is due to end at 07:00 GMT on Saturday.

But consultants and specialist doctors will begin a separate 24-hour strike on Monday, as part of the same pay dispute.

The British Medical Association (BMA) rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise and wants to restore the value of doctors' pay to 2008 levels.

Health Minister, Robbie Butler, said he had accepted the recommended rise but could not implement it without sufficient funding for his department.

Friday's strike action by resident doctors affected non-emergency services, resulting in the cancellation of many planned outpatient appointments.

Urgent surgery and most GP services continued as normal because senior doctors remained on duty.

How will patients be affected on Monday?

Monday's walkout will involve consultants and specialty, associate specialist and specialist grade (SAS) doctors and will also take place over 24 hours from 07:00 on Monday.

Routine hospital and elective services are expected to be cancelled during the second strike.

But emergency care will continue under Christmas Day cover - which means full emergency cover will remain in place.

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The South Eastern Trust said the urgent care centre at Lagan Valley Hospital would be closed on Monday and that postponed appointments and procedures would be rescheduled as soon as possible.

Butler said more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled during similar strikes in June and warned the latest action would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery".

Why are doctors striking?

The BMA says years of below-inflation pay rises have made it harder for Northern Ireland's health service to recruit and retain doctors.

Dr Seamus Crumley, an anaesthetics registrar who works in intensive care at the Ulster Hospital, joined Friday's picket line in Belfast.

He told BBC News NI he had taken a pay cut when he moved from Scotland last year, despite securing a more senior role.

"The medical workforce here is very, very vulnerable to losing doctors to literally anywhere else in the UK, but also to the Republic of Ireland," he said.

Dr Steven Montgomery, who chairs the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said his colleagues were facing burnout and emotional distress because of pressure at work.

He said the union was "not looking for this all to be paid in one lump sum" and wanted the minister to set out a plan to restore pay over time.

Dr OisÃn Fearon, a resident doctor in Belfast, told BBC News NI he had considered moving to Australia, but family and local ties had kept him in Northern Ireland.

He said he had begun the process of registering to train in the Republic of Ireland and was keeping that option open.

What has the health minister said?

Butler said he had met the BMA to explain the financial pressures facing his department, external and intended to implement the recommended award as soon as possible.

He said cumulative pay rises over the previous three years averaged 30% for resident doctors, 25% for SAS doctors and 24% for consultants.

Butler said the recommended rise was higher than that for other healthcare staff and warned that going beyond 3.5% would have "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

Separately, the Northern Ireland Public Service Alliance (Nipsa) released the results of a recent ballot of its health and social care members.

It said 94% of its health and social care members backed strike action, while 97% backed action short of a strike, over growing pressures on the health and social care sector.

The union said it would consider its next steps and warned that coordinated industrial action could spread across the health service in the coming weeks.

item.title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
item.description:

Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm

- Published

Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.

Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."

Next says its own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is under way.

Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."

Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.

They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."

To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.

For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.

Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.

After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.

"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"

Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.

Check the gap around the neck

Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.

She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.

"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.

"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"

Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.

But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.

The Lullaby Trust is a UK charity that works to prevent sudden, unexpected infant deaths, including SIDS.

CEO Jenny Ward told BBC News that the charity could not comment on the safety of specific products, since it does not carry out independent product safety testing.

But she encourages families to check that any product they use has passed the necessary safety checks and meets British Safety Standards.

She said: "Remember to follow the manufacturer's instructions and if a family is worried about any product we would say to stop using it and contact the manufacturer.

"We support the Office for Product Safety and Standards' recent warning on certain baby sleep bags and would urge families to ensure a sleep bag fits well before they use it."

People can check if any products have been recalled by visiting the OPSS website, external.
